chapters.1: David learns of Saul and Jonathan's deaths from an Amalekite messenger who claims to have killed Saul at his own request, and David has the man executed for killing the Lord's anointed. David then composes a heartfelt lament mourning both Saul and his beloved friend Jonathan.
chapters.2: David is anointed king over Judah at Hebron, while Saul's surviving son Ishbosheth is made king over the rest of Israel with the backing of Saul's general Abner. Tension between the two camps erupts into conflict, including a duel-like skirmish where Abner kills Joab's brother Asahel in self-defense during a retreat.
chapters.3: As David's power grows and Ishbosheth's weakens, Abner eventually seeks to defect to David's side, bringing the rest of Israel with him. Before the alliance is finalized, Joab murders Abner in revenge for his brother's death, and David publicly mourns Abner and distances himself from the killing.
chapters.4: With Abner dead, Ishbosheth's support collapses further, and two of his own captains, Baanah and Rechab, assassinate him and bring his head to David expecting a reward. Instead, David has them executed for murdering an innocent man, maintaining his pattern of refusing to profit from violence against Saul's house.
chapters.5: All the tribes of Israel come to David at Hebron and anoint him king over the whole nation, uniting Israel and Judah under one ruler. David then captures Jerusalem from the Jebusites, makes it his capital, and defeats the Philistines in battle with God's help.
chapters.6: David organizes a procession to bring the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, but the celebration turns tragic when Uzzah is struck down for improperly touching the ark. After a pause, David successfully brings the ark into the city with great rejoicing, though his wife Michal despises him for dancing exuberantly before the Lord.
chapters.7: David wants to build a permanent temple for God, but the prophet Nathan delivers a message from God declining the offer for now and instead promising David an everlasting dynasty, with his descendants ruling forever. David responds with a humble and grateful prayer of thanksgiving for this covenant promise.
chapters.8: David wins a series of military victories over neighboring nations, including the Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, and the Arameans of Zobah, greatly expanding Israel's territory and wealth. The chapter summarizes David's successful, God-blessed reign and lists his key officials.
chapters.9: Remembering his covenant of friendship with Jonathan, David seeks out Jonathan's surviving son, Mephibosheth, who is disabled, and shows him great kindness by restoring Saul's land to him and inviting him to eat permanently at the king's own table.
chapters.10: David sends envoys to express condolences to the new Ammonite king Hanun, but Hanun's advisors convince him to humiliate David's men instead, triggering a war. Israel defeats the combined forces of Ammon and their hired Syrian allies under the command of Joab and his brother Abishai.
chapters.11: David commits adultery with Bathsheba, the wife of his soldier Uriah, while Uriah is away at war, and when she becomes pregnant, David arranges to have Uriah killed in battle to cover up the affair. David then takes Bathsheba as his wife, but the chapter notes that what he did displeased the Lord.
chapters.12: The prophet Nathan confronts David with a parable about a rich man stealing a poor man's beloved lamb, exposing David's sin with Bathsheba and Uriah; David confesses and repents, but Nathan announces serious consequences, including the death of the child born from the affair. Bathsheba later bears another son, Solomon, and David also achieves victory over the Ammonite capital of Rabbah.
chapters.13: David's son Amnon becomes obsessed with his half-sister Tamar and, with a friend's scheming help, lures her into a situation where he rapes her, then coldly rejects her. Tamar's full brother Absalom harbors deep anger over this and, two years later, has Amnon murdered in revenge, then flees into exile.
chapters.14: Joab arranges for a wise woman to tell David a parable designed to persuade him to allow Absalom to return from exile, and David agrees, though he initially keeps Absalom away from his presence. After some time, Absalom is fully restored to the king's favor and reconciled with his father, though underlying tensions remain.
chapters.15: Absalom begins quietly building political support and eventually launches an open rebellion against his father, declaring himself king at Hebron. David is forced to flee Jerusalem with his loyal followers, weeping as he leaves the city, and he sends the priest Hushai back as a secret informant within Absalom's camp.
chapters.16: As David flees Jerusalem, he encounters conflicting loyalty from Saul's household: Ziba brings him provisions while claiming Mephibosheth has betrayed him, and Shimei curses and throws stones at David, which David tolerates as possibly deserved judgment from God. Meanwhile, Absalom enters Jerusalem and publicly takes his father's concubines to assert his claim to the throne.
chapters.17: Absalom's advisors Ahithophel and Hushai give conflicting military advice on how to pursue David; Absalom follows Hushai's more cautious counsel, which buys David crucial time to escape across the Jordan. Ahithophel, realizing his advice was rejected and the rebellion may fail, goes home and takes his own life.
chapters.18: David's forces meet Absalom's rebel army in the forest of Ephraim, where David's side wins decisively, and despite David's explicit order to spare his son, Joab has Absalom killed after finding him caught in a tree by his hair. A messenger brings David the news of victory, but David is overwhelmed with grief upon learning of Absalom's death.
chapters.19: Joab rebukes David for mourning Absalom so publicly that it demoralizes the very soldiers who risked their lives for him, prompting David to compose himself and address his troops. David then begins the delicate process of returning to Jerusalem and reconciling with various people, including Shimei and Mephibosheth, amid renewed tension between Judah and the rest of Israel.
chapters.20: A Benjamite named Sheba leads a fresh rebellion against David, drawing much of Israel away from him temporarily, while Joab ruthlessly kills his rival commander Amasa during the pursuit. Joab's forces besiege Sheba in the city of Abel, where a wise local woman negotiates Sheba's death to end the siege peacefully.
chapters.21: A three-year famine is revealed to be judgment for Saul's earlier massacre of the Gibeonites, so David hands over seven of Saul's descendants to be executed to make amends, while sparing Mephibosheth. The chapter also recounts several battles against Philistine giants, including Goliath's relatives, fought by David's mighty men.
chapters.22: This chapter contains a lengthy song of David praising God as his rock, fortress, and deliverer, celebrating God's rescue of him from enemies and from the brink of death throughout his life. It closely parallels the content of Psalm 18 and reflects David's gratitude near the end of his reign.
chapters.23: David offers a final poetic reflection on God's covenant with his house and the character of righteous rule, followed by a detailed roll call honoring his "mighty men," an elite group of warriors known for extraordinary feats of courage in his service.
chapters.24: David orders a census of Israel in a moment of pride that displeases God, and as judgment he is given a choice of three punishments, choosing a plague that kills many people. The book closes with David buying a threshing floor from Araunah the Jebusite and building an altar there to stop the plague, a site that later becomes the location of the temple.
